title: Straight Stair
description: A straight stair runs in one flight from one floor to the next, and it is the simplest stair to lay out because every riser and tread is the same. The layout starts from the total rise, the vertical distance between finished floors, divided into equal risers no higher than the local code maximum, commonly 7-3/4 inches. Keep every riser within 3/8 inch of the others, because an uneven riser is what trips people. The stringers carry the stair, the treads sit on them, and a landing or floor at each end gives a safe place to step on and off.

image.description: Diagram shows a straight stair flight with 14 risers at 7.5 in and 10 in treads, with total rise dimensioned.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Straight Stair</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Total rise 105 in; 14 risers at 7.5 in; tread run 10 in; sta</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Total rise 105 in; 14 risers at 7.5 in; tread run 10 in; stair width 36 in
specs.tolerances: Riser variation under 3/8 in; tread level within 1/16 in
specs.load_notes: Residential stair loads; stringers sized per span tables.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: stair: 14 risers at 7.50 in each, total run 130.0 in, stringer 167.1 in

cut_list.dimensions: 144 in long (cut) x 9-1/4 in x 1-1/2 in

steps: Measure the total rise between finished floors at both stringer positions.
Divide the total rise into equal risers at or under the maximum allowed.
Lay out the stringers with a framing square, marking rise and run at each step.
Cut the stringers, test-fit them, and fasten them plumb and level.
Install risers, then treads with adhesive and screws, checking each tread level.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

demo.code:
TOTAL_RISE = 105.0
MAX_RISE = 7.75
RUN = 10.00
import math
RISERS = math.ceil(TOTAL_RISE / MAX_RISE)
RISE = TOTAL_RISE / RISERS
TOTAL_RUN = RUN * (RISERS - 1)
STRINGER = math.hypot(TOTAL_RUN, TOTAL_RISE)
print("Total rise: %.1f in, max rise: %.2f in" % (TOTAL_RISE, MAX_RISE))
print("Risers: %d" % RISERS)
print("Actual rise each: %.2f in" % RISE)
print("Total run: %.1f in" % TOTAL_RUN)
print("Stringer length: %.1f in" % STRINGER)
demo.expected_output:
Total rise: 105.0 in, max rise: 7.75 in
Risers: 14
Actual rise each: 7.50 in
Total run: 130.0 in
Stringer length: 167.1 in

title: L-Stair Basics
description: An L-stair turns 90 degrees at a landing, which lets a stair fit a corner and breaks a long climb into two shorter flights. The landing is the key: it must be at least as wide as the stair and deep enough to step onto comfortably, and both flights must meet it with the same riser height so the rhythm of the climb never changes. Lay out the lower flight, the landing height, and the upper flight as one calculation, not as two separate stairs, or the risers will disagree at the landing and trip the climber.

image.description: Diagram shows two stair flights meeting at a square 36 in landing, turning 90 degrees.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">L-Stair Basics</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Two flights; landing 36 in x 36 in; risers 7.5 in each fligh</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Two flights; landing 36 in x 36 in; risers 7.5 in each flight; stair width 36 in
specs.tolerances: Riser variation under 3/8 in across both flights; landing level within 1/16 in
specs.load_notes: Residential stair loads; landing framed to carry both flights.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: stair: 7 risers at 7.50 in each, total run 60.0 in, stringer 79.7 in

cut_list.dimensions: cut to flight length x 9-1/4 in x 1-1/2 in

steps: Measure the total rise and plan the landing height so both flights share one riser height.
Frame the landing level, square, and at least as wide as the stair.
Lay out and cut the lower flight stringers to meet the landing.
Lay out and cut the upper flight stringers from the landing to the upper floor.
Install treads on both flights, checking the riser rhythm across the landing.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

RISE = TOTAL_RISE / RISERS

print("Risers: %d" % RISERS)

title: Stair Handrail
description: A stair handrail gives a continuous grip from the bottom of the stair to the top, and it is a safety device first and a trim piece second. The rail height is measured vertically from the nosing line, commonly 34 to 38 inches, and the rail must run continuously without breaks that force a hand to let go. Balusters, the vertical spindles under the rail, are spaced so that a 4 inch sphere cannot pass between them, which keeps small children from slipping through. Fasten the rail solidly into studs or blocking; a rail that wobbles is worse than no rail at all in a fall.

image.description: Diagram shows a sloped handrail 36 in above the stair nosings, with balusters spaced under 4 in apart.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Stair Handrail</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Rail height 36 in above nosings; stair width 36 in; baluster</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Rail height 36 in above nosings; stair width 36 in; baluster spacing under 4 in
specs.tolerances: Baluster gaps under 4 in; rail height 34 to 38 in above nosings
specs.load_notes: Handrail must resist a 200 lb concentrated load per common code practice.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: balusters: 18 intervals over 72.0 in at max 4.0 in gap = 17 balusters at 4.00 in spacing

steps: Mark the rail height above the nosings at the top and bottom of the flight.
Set the newel posts plumb and fasten them solidly to framing.
Cut the handrail to length with matching angle cuts at each end.
Space the balusters evenly, keeping every gap under 4 inches.
Fasten the rail and balusters, then test the rail for any wobble.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

demo.code:
L = 72.0
MAXGAP = 4.0
import math
INTERVALS = math.ceil(L / MAXGAP)
SPACING = L / INTERVALS
BALUSTERS = INTERVALS - 1
print("Rail length: %.1f in, max gap: %.1f in" % (L, MAXGAP))
print("Intervals: %d" % INTERVALS)
print("Balusters needed: %d" % BALUSTERS)
print("Actual spacing: %.2f in" % SPACING)
demo.expected_output:
Rail length: 72.0 in, max gap: 4.0 in
Intervals: 18
Balusters needed: 17
Actual spacing: 4.00 in

title: Interior Door Hanging
description: Hanging an interior door means fitting a pre-hung or slab door into its frame so it swings freely, latches cleanly, and shows even gaps, called reveals, of about 1/8 inch on the sides and top. Start with the frame: it must be plumb, level, and square, or no amount of planing the door will fix the swing. Hang the door on its hinges first, check the reveals, then mark and cut the latch and strike positions. A door that is planed to fit a crooked frame will bind again when the seasons change.

image.description: Diagram shows a door in its frame with 1/8 in reveals marked on the sides and top.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Interior Door Hanging</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Door 30 in x 80 in x 1-3/8 in; reveals 1/8 in; rough opening</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Door 30 in x 80 in x 1-3/8 in; reveals 1/8 in; rough opening 32 in x 82-1/2 in
specs.tolerances: Reveals 1/8 in, even within 1/32 in; frame plumb within 1/16 in
specs.load_notes: Interior use only; no weather or security loads.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: rough opening 30.0 in + 2 in = 32.0 in wide, 80.0 in + 2.5 in = 82.5 in high

steps: Check the frame for plumb, level, and square, shimming it true.
Mark and mortise the hinge positions on the door edge and jamb.
Screw the hinges to the door, then hang the door on the jamb.
Check the reveals and plane the door edge only where it binds.
Mark, drill, and fit the latch and strike plate, then test the swing.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection, cut away from the body, keep chisels and knives sharp so they do not slip, and clamp the work before cutting or paring.

demo.code:
DOOR_W = 30.0
DOOR_H = 80.0
RW = DOOR_W + 2.0
RH = DOOR_H + 2.5
print("Door: %.1f in x %.1f in" % (DOOR_W, DOOR_H))
print("Width allowance: 2.0 in")
print("Height allowance: 2.5 in")
print("Rough opening: %.1f in wide x %.1f in high" % (RW, RH))
demo.expected_output:
Door: 30.0 in x 80.0 in
Width allowance: 2.0 in
Height allowance: 2.5 in
Rough opening: 32.0 in wide x 82.5 in high

title: Exterior Door Frame
description: An exterior door frame must do everything an interior frame does, plus keep out weather, so it is built with a sill, weatherstripping, and flashing that sheds water outward. The rough opening is framed about 2 inches wider and 2-1/2 inches taller than the door unit to leave room for shims and the sill, and the sill sits on a bed of sealant over flashing, never directly on bare framing. Set the hinge side plumb first, shim the frame true, and check the door against its weatherstripping before foaming or trimming, because a frame foamed out of square is very hard to correct.

image.description: Diagram shows an exterior door frame with sill sloping outward, flashing, and weatherstripping contact.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Exterior Door Frame</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Door unit 36 in x 80 in; rough opening 38 in x 82-1/2 in; si</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Door unit 36 in x 80 in; rough opening 38 in x 82-1/2 in; sill with 5 degree slope outward
specs.tolerances: Frame plumb within 1/16 in; sill sloped outward; weatherstrip contact even
specs.load_notes: Exterior weather exposure; sill must drain outward.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: rough opening 36.0 in + 2 in = 38.0 in wide, 80.0 in + 2.5 in = 82.5 in high

steps: Flash the opening and bed the sill in sealant with an outward slope.
Set the unit in the opening, hinge side plumb first, and shim it true.
Check the door closes evenly against the weatherstripping.
Fasten through the shims into framing on both sides.
Foam the gaps with low-expansion foam, then trim and seal the exterior.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

print("Door: %.1f in x %.1f in" % (DOOR_W, DOOR_H))
print("Width allowance: 2.0 in")

title: Sliding Barn Door
description: A sliding barn door hangs from a wall-mounted rail and slides sideways instead of swinging, which saves floor space but needs a solid wall and a level rail. The rail must fasten into studs or a header board, because a door hanging from drywall anchors alone will pull out. The rail length is at least twice the door width so the door can slide fully clear of the opening, and floor guides keep the bottom from swinging. Hang the door, check it rolls freely and stays on the rail at both ends, and fit soft stops so it cannot roll off.

image.description: Diagram shows a barn door on a 72 in wall rail, sliding clear of a 36 in opening, with a floor guide.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Sliding Barn Door</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Door 36 in x 84 in x 1-3/8 in; rail 72 in long; wall clearan</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Door 36 in x 84 in x 1-3/8 in; rail 72 in long; wall clearance 1/2 in
specs.tolerances: Rail level within 1/16 in over its length; door clears the floor by 1/2 in
specs.load_notes: Door weight carried by rail into studs; check hanger rating against door weight.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: area 36.0 in x 84.0 in = 3024.0 square inches

steps: Locate the studs and fasten the header board level into them.
Mount the rail to the header, checking it level end to end.
Fit the hangers to the door top and hang the door on the rail.
Fit the floor guide and check the door slides fully clear of the opening.
Fit end stops and soft closers, then test the full travel.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

print("Size: %.1f in x %.1f in" % (L, W))
print("Area: %.1f square inches" % AREA)

Area: 3024.0 square inches

title: Window Frame Build
description: Building a window frame means making a square, rigid box that holds a sash true and keeps weather out: a head at the top, a sill at the bottom sloped to shed water, and jambs on the sides, all joined with weather-resistant joinery. The sill slope is the detail that matters most, because a flat sill holds water against the wall and rots the frame. Build the frame on a flat bench, check both diagonals equal before the glue sets, and size the opening so the frame fits with a small, even shim gap all around.

image.description: Diagram shows a window frame with a sloped sill at the bottom and jambs, head, and sill labeled.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Window Frame Build</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Frame 36 in x 48 in; sill slope 5 degrees outward; jamb stoc</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Frame 36 in x 48 in; sill slope 5 degrees outward; jamb stock 3/4 in thick
specs.tolerances: Frame diagonals equal within 1/16 in; sill sloped outward
specs.load_notes: Exterior weather exposure; sill must drain outward.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: true diagonal of 36.0 in x 48.0 in = 60.00 in, measured 60.00 in, error 0.00 in

steps: Cut the jambs, head, and sill, sloping the sill outward.
Join the frame on a flat bench with glue and screws.
Check both diagonals equal and the frame square before the glue sets.
Fit the frame into the opening with even shim gaps.
Seal the exterior joints and check the sill drains clear of the wall.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

demo.code:
A = 36.0
B = 48.0
MEAS = 60.00
import math
DIAG = math.hypot(A, B)
ERR = MEAS - DIAG
print("Sides: %.1f in x %.1f in" % (A, B))
print("True diagonal: %.2f in" % DIAG)
print("Measured diagonal: %.2f in" % MEAS)
print("Error: %.2f in" % ERR)
print("Square verdict: %s" % ("square within 1/16 in" if abs(ERR) <= 0.0625 else "out of square, adjust"))
demo.expected_output:
Sides: 36.0 in x 48.0 in
True diagonal: 60.00 in
Measured diagonal: 60.00 in
Error: 0.00 in
Square verdict: square within 1/16 in

title: Window Sash Repair
description: Repairing a window sash means restoring a sash that sticks, rattles, or will not stay up, usually by fixing its cords or springs, its glazing, and its fit in the frame. Start by finding the cause: paint bridging the sash to the frame, a broken cord, or swollen wood each need a different fix, and planing a sash that only needs its cords replaced wastes a good sash. Free painted joints with a knife, replace cords or balances in pairs so both sides pull evenly, and re-glaze loose panes with putty bedded under the glass edge.

image.description: Diagram shows a window sash with cords, pulleys, and a glazed pane, with the putty bevel marked.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Window Sash Repair</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Sash 30 in x 36 in x 1-3/8 in; cord pair; glazing putty bed </text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Sash 30 in x 36 in x 1-3/8 in; cord pair; glazing putty bed 1/8 in
specs.tolerances: Sash slides freely with 1/16 in clearance per side; cords equal length within 1/4 in
specs.load_notes: Window use only; balance weights must match sash weight.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: area 30.0 in x 36.0 in = 1080.0 square inches

steps: Free any paint bridging the sash to the frame with a knife.
Remove the sash and inspect cords, pulleys, and glazing.
Replace cords or balances in matched pairs.
Re-bed loose glass in putty, pin it, and tool a clean putty bevel.
Rehang the sash, check it slides and stays put, and touch up paint.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection, cut away from the body, keep chisels and knives sharp so they do not slip, and clamp the work before cutting or paring.

print("Area: %.1f square inches" % AREA)

title: Door Casing and Trim
description: Door casing is the trim that covers the gap between the door frame and the wall, and a clean casing job is mostly a miter job: two side casings and a head casing joined at 45 degree miters at the top corners. Cut the head casing first, then the sides, and keep the reveal, the small step of jamb showing beside the casing, even all around, usually about 1/4 inch. Nail the casing to the jamb and to the wall framing, not only to one or the other, or seasonal movement will open the miters. A tiny bead of glue on the miter faces keeps the corners closed.

image.description: Diagram shows door casing with a 1/4 in reveal and 45 degree miters at the head corners.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Door Casing and Trim</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Casing 2-1/4 in wide x 3/4 in thick; reveal 1/4 in; head mit</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Casing 2-1/4 in wide x 3/4 in thick; reveal 1/4 in; head miters 45 degrees
specs.tolerances: Reveal even 1/4 in within 1/32 in; miters closed, no gap
specs.load_notes: Interior trim only; no structural load.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: two miter cuts of 45.00 degrees sum to 90.0 degrees

steps: Mark the 1/4 in reveal line around the jamb.
Cut the head casing with 45 degree miters at both ends.
Cut the side casings with matching top miters.
Nail the casing along the reveal line into jamb and framing.
Check the miters closed, fill nail holes, and sand lightly.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

print("Joint angle: %.1f degrees" % JOINT_DEG)
print("Miter cut per piece: %.2f degrees" % MITER_DEG)
print("Check: two miters sum to %.1f degrees" % (MITER_DEG * 2.0))
demo.expected_output:

Joint angle: 90.0 degrees
Miter cut per piece: 45.00 degrees
Check: two miters sum to 90.0 degrees

title: Stair Tread Replacement
description: Replacing a stair tread means removing one worn or split tread without damaging the stringers, then fitting a new tread tight and level. Cut the old tread out in pieces if it is glued and nailed, working from the middle outward so the stringer housings are not pried apart. Fit the new tread by scribing it to the stringers if they are not perfectly parallel, and fasten it with adhesive and screws from below where possible so the walking surface shows no fasteners. Check the new tread is level and its nosing lines up with its neighbors, or the step will feel wrong underfoot.

image.description: Diagram shows a single replacement tread fitted between two stringers, with the 1 in nosing marked.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Stair Tread Replacement</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Tread 36 in x 10 in x 1 in; nosing overhang 1 in; replacemen</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Tread 36 in x 10 in x 1 in; nosing overhang 1 in; replacement fits existing stringers
specs.tolerances: Tread level within 1/16 in; nosing aligned within 1/16 in of neighbors
specs.load_notes: Residential stair loads; tread must bear on both stringers.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: board feet for 1.00 in x 10.0 in x 36.0 in = 2.500

steps: Protect the neighboring treads and cut the old tread out in pieces.
Clean the stringer housings without prying them apart.
Scribe and cut the new tread to fit the actual stringer spacing.
Bed the tread in adhesive and screw it from below.
Check level and nosing alignment, then finish to match.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

W = 10.0
L = 36.0
BF = T * W * L / 144.0
print("Board: %.2f in thick x %.1f in wide x %.1f in long" % (T, W, L))
print("Board feet: %.3f" % BF)

title: Basement Stair
description: A basement stair must handle headroom, moisture, and a concrete landing, three things an ordinary interior stair often avoids. Headroom is the first check: the stair needs a clear height above every tread, and a basement stair that ducks under a low beam is a hazard every day. Concrete at the bottom needs a treated bottom step or a moisture break so the stringer ends do not wick water and rot, and the bottom of the stair must land on a solid, level pad. Lay the stair out from the finished basement floor upward, keeping the risers equal all the way to the top floor.

image.description: Diagram shows a basement stair descending to a concrete pad, with headroom clearance marked above the treads.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Basement Stair</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Total rise 96 in; 13 risers at about 7.38 in; tread run 10 i</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Total rise 96 in; 13 risers at about 7.38 in; tread run 10 in; width 36 in
specs.tolerances: Headroom clear above every tread; riser variation under 3/8 in
specs.load_notes: Residential stair loads; bottom stringer ends protected from moisture.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: stair: 13 risers at 7.38 in each, total run 120.0 in, stringer 153.7 in

cut_list.dimensions: cut to length x 9-1/4 in x 1-1/2 in

steps: Check headroom above every tread position before cutting anything.
Prepare a level concrete pad and a moisture break at the stair foot.
Lay out the stringers from the finished basement floor upward.
Cut, fit, and fasten the stringers, protecting the treated ends.
Install risers and treads, checking riser rhythm to the top floor.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

demo.code:
TOTAL_RISE = 96.0
MAX_RISE = 7.75
RUN = 10.00
import math
RISERS = math.ceil(TOTAL_RISE / MAX_RISE)
RISE = TOTAL_RISE / RISERS
TOTAL_RUN = RUN * (RISERS - 1)
STRINGER = math.hypot(TOTAL_RUN, TOTAL_RISE)
print("Total rise: %.1f in, max rise: %.2f in" % (TOTAL_RISE, MAX_RISE))
print("Risers: %d" % RISERS)
print("Actual rise each: %.2f in" % RISE)
print("Total run: %.1f in" % TOTAL_RUN)
print("Stringer length: %.1f in" % STRINGER)
demo.expected_output:
Total rise: 96.0 in, max rise: 7.75 in
Risers: 13
Actual rise each: 7.38 in
Total run: 120.0 in
Stringer length: 153.7 in

title: Attic Stair and Ladder
description: An attic stair or pull-down ladder gives access through a ceiling opening without giving up floor space, and its safety depends on the opening size, the ladder angle, and a solid ceiling frame. The rough opening must match the unit, and the ceiling joists around it need headers so the opening does not weaken the ceiling. Install the unit level and square in the opening, fasten it into the headers, and check the ladder feet sit flat on the floor below with the sections locking fully open. A ladder that rocks or does not lock is not finished.

image.description: Diagram shows a pull-down attic ladder through a 25 in by 54 in ceiling opening, at about 75 degrees.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Attic Stair and Ladder</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Rough opening 25 in x 54 in; ceiling height 96 in; ladder an</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Rough opening 25 in x 54 in; ceiling height 96 in; ladder angle about 75 degrees
specs.tolerances: Unit level within 1/16 in; ladder feet flat; sections lock fully
specs.load_notes: Attic access loads per unit rating; never exceed the unit weight rating.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: area 25.0 in x 54.0 in = 1350.0 square inches

steps: Frame the ceiling opening with headers sized for the unit.
Lift the unit into the opening and shim it level and square.
Fasten the unit into the headers on all sides.
Open the ladder fully and check the feet sit flat and sections lock.
Trim the opening and test the ladder through several open-close cycles.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye and hearing protection, keep hands clear of blades and cutters, unplug tools before changing blades or bits, and never reach across a running blade. Work at a steady feed rate and use push sticks and guards where the tool provides them.

demo.code:

W = 54.0

print("Size: %.1f in x %.1f in" % (L, W))
print("Area: %.1f square inches" % AREA)

title: French Door Pair
description: A French door pair is two glazed doors that meet in the middle, and its success depends on the pair meeting evenly: both doors must hang plumb, the meeting stiles must close together without a gap, and the astragal or flush bolts must hold the inactive door firm. Hang the active door first and get it swinging and latching cleanly, then fit the inactive door to it, not to the frame alone. Weatherstripping at the meeting stiles matters as much as at the frame, because the middle joint is where exterior pairs leak first.

image.description: Diagram shows a pair of glazed doors meeting at center stiles, with the meeting gap dimensioned.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">French Door Pair</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Each door 30 in x 80 in x 1-3/4 in; rough opening 62 in x 82</text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Each door 30 in x 80 in x 1-3/4 in; rough opening 62 in x 82-1/2 in; meeting stile gap under 1/8 in
specs.tolerances: Meeting stile gap under 1/8 in; both doors plumb within 1/16 in
specs.load_notes: Exterior pairs need full weatherstripping at the meeting stiles.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: rough opening 60.0 in + 2 in = 62.0 in wide, 80.0 in + 2.5 in = 82.5 in high

steps: Set the frame plumb, level, and square, and shim it true.
Hang the active door and check its swing, reveals, and latch.
Hang the inactive door to meet the active door evenly.
Fit the astragal and flush bolts so the inactive door holds firm.
Fit weatherstripping at the meeting stiles and test both doors.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection, cut away from the body, keep chisels and knives sharp so they do not slip, and clamp the work before cutting or paring.

demo.code:
DOOR_W = 60.0
DOOR_H = 80.0
RW = DOOR_W + 2.0
RH = DOOR_H + 2.5
print("Door: %.1f in x %.1f in" % (DOOR_W, DOOR_H))
print("Width allowance: 2.0 in")
print("Height allowance: 2.5 in")
print("Rough opening: %.1f in wide x %.1f in high" % (RW, RH))
demo.expected_output:

Width allowance: 2.0 in
Height allowance: 2.5 in
Rough opening: 62.0 in wide x 82.5 in high

title: Screen Door
description: A screen door lets air through while keeping insects out, and it hangs on the outside of an exterior door frame on hinges with a closer that pulls it shut. The frame must be square and the door must clear the threshold, because a screen door that drags will not close and a closer cannot fix a binding door. Fit the hinges, then the latch, then adjust the closer so the door closes fully but does not slam. Replace torn screen mesh by removing the spline, laying new mesh flat, and rolling a new spline into the groove.

image.description: Diagram shows a screen door with mesh, spline groove, hinges, and a closer arm.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Screen Door</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Door 32 in x 80 in x 1 in; closer sweep adjustable; mesh 18 </text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Door 32 in x 80 in x 1 in; closer sweep adjustable; mesh 18 x 14 per inch
specs.tolerances: Door clears threshold by 1/4 in; closer closes door fully without slamming
specs.load_notes: Light exterior use; closer must not slam the door.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: area 32.0 in x 80.0 in = 2560.0 square inches

steps: Check the frame square and the threshold clearance.
Hang the door on its hinges and check it swings without binding.
Fit the latch and strike and test the latching.
Fit and adjust the closer for a full, gentle close.
For torn mesh, replace the spline and mesh and trim the excess.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection, cut away from the body, keep chisels and knives sharp so they do not slip, and clamp the work before cutting or paring.

Area: 2560.0 square inches

title: Window Seat Frame
description: A window seat frame is a low box built under a window that gives seating and storage, and it must be built like a small cabinet: level, square, and strong enough to sit on. Frame it with a plywood top that overhangs the front slightly as a nosing, and leave the front open or fitted with doors or drawers for storage. The top height is a sitting height, about 18 to 19 inches including the cushion, and the frame must be fastened to the wall studs so it cannot tip forward when someone sits on its edge.

image.description: Diagram shows a window seat box 48 in wide and 18 in high under a window, with a 1 in top overhang.

specs.tolerances: Frame level within 1/16 in; top height 18 to 19 in with cushion
specs.load_notes: Seating loads; frame fastened to wall studs.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: area 48.0 in x 18.0 in = 864.0 square inches

Build the box frame square on a flat surface.
Fasten the frame to the wall studs and check it level.
Fit the seat top with a 1 in front overhang.
Fit doors or drawers if planned, then the cushion.

title: Door Threshold
description: A door threshold is the strip under an exterior door that bridges the gap between inside and outside floors and sheds water away from the house. It must sit level across the door width, slope slightly outward, and seal to the door bottom with a sweep or weatherstrip, or wind-driven rain will find the gap. Remove the old threshold without damaging the jambs, bed the new one in sealant, and fasten it into the framing below. Check the door closes over it without dragging and the sweep contacts evenly along its length.

image.description: Diagram shows a threshold under a door, sloping outward with a sweep contacting its top.
image.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 220" width="400" height="220"><rect width="400" height="220" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="20" y="30" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">Door Threshold</text><polyline points="30,180 30,150 90,150 90,120 150,120 150,90 210,90 210,60 270,60 270,30 370,30" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="30" y1="195" x2="370" y2="195" stroke="#333"/><text x="30" y="212" font-size="13">Threshold 36 in wide x 5 in deep; outward slope 1/8 in over </text></svg>

specs.dimensions: Threshold 36 in wide x 5 in deep; outward slope 1/8 in over the depth; door bottom clearance 1/4 in
specs.tolerances: Threshold level across width; sloped outward; sweep contact even
specs.load_notes: Foot traffic and weather exposure; threshold must not rock.
specs.arithmetic_note: Numbers check: threshold slope 0.125 in over 5.00 in = 0.0250 in per in, angle 1.43 degrees

steps: Remove the old threshold carefully, protecting the jambs.
Clean and dry the sill area and check it level.
Bed the new threshold in sealant with a slight outward slope.
Fasten it into the framing and seal the ends.
Fit the door sweep and check the door closes without dragging.

tools.safety_notes: Wear eye protection, cut away from the body, keep chisels and knives sharp so they do not slip, and clamp the work before cutting or paring.

demo.code:
DEPTH = 5.00
DROP = 0.125
import math
SLOPE = DROP / DEPTH
ANGLE = math.degrees(math.atan(SLOPE))
print("Depth: %.2f in, drop: %.3f in" % (DEPTH, DROP))
print("Slope: %.4f in per in" % SLOPE)
print("Slope angle: %.2f degrees" % ANGLE)
demo.expected_output:
Depth: 5.00 in, drop: 0.125 in
Slope: 0.0250 in per in
Slope angle: 1.43 degrees
